🇷🇴 🇷🇺 🇲🇩 🇪🇺 People from Kadyrov’s inner circle and a former top manager of Gazprom obtained Romanian passports using forged documents, according to an international investigation. Some of them pretended to be Ukrainians in order to get EU citizenship. Journalists from the French newspaper Le Monde, the Moldovan outlet Cu Sens and other media examined 55 court cases on the annulment of Romanian documents that had been issued on the basis of forgeries. In more than 30 cases the recipients turned out to be Russians, including businessmen under EU sanctions and people connected to organized crime. At least eight Russian citizens used Ukrainian passports and fake certificates of Romanian citizenship to obtain genuine Romanian documents in 2023–2024. The scheme exploited a law that allows descendants of residents of former Romanian territories to restore their Romanian citizenship. According to Le Monde’s sources, this service could cost from 50 to 70 thousand euros. Middlemen in Romania and notaries in Moldova were involved in arranging the paperwork. Some of the recipients were registered only on paper in the small Romanian village of Vârful Câmpului, which had around three thousand residents in 2011 but now has more than 12 thousand people registered. One local resident admitted to journalists that he registered foreigners at his house for 50 euros. At one point, thousands of people were listed at a single address. Among the figures mentioned in the investigation is the former general director of Gazprom Mezhregiongaz, Kirill Seleznev, who is under US and UK sanctions. In December 2023 his documents were entered into the Romanian registries on the basis of a forged citizenship certificate. In February 2026 a court in Bucharest annulled these records. Another figure is Mayrbek Abdulazizov from Ramzan Kadyrov’s entourage. He works as an adviser to his brother, who heads the territorial compulsory health insurance fund of Chechnya, and in 2024 he received the Kadyrov Order. To obtain Romanian documents, Abdulazizov used a Ukrainian passport and a citizenship certificate supposedly issued by the Romanian consulate in Istanbul, but bearing the stamp of the embassy in Bratislava. The address in Kyiv that he provided turned out not to exist — journalists found an empty lot there. The journalists also found documents belonging to Nurutdin Dadaev, a native of Dagestan who is regarded as a “thief in law” both in Russia and in Ukraine. The documents obtained allowed their holders to move freely around the European Union, open bank accounts and register companies. The Romanian authorities are investigating hundreds of similar cases and are trying to annul the illegally issued documents. More than 800 court cases related to their cancellation are currently being examined.

Interview: UK Defense Secretary on 'nauseating' Putin The U.K.'s Defense Secretary Wes Streeting has described Russian President Vladimir Putin's appearance at a trilateral summit with his Chinese and U.S. counterparts as "nauseating." "The nauseating thing about the last week is you've got Putin out there talking about peace, not wanting war, walking up red carpets, and at the same time his war machine is raining missiles down on civilian targets here in Kyiv and right across Ukraine," he told the Kyiv Independent in an interview in Kyiv on Nov. 23.
